title: The compiler picks an overload from the static type

blocks.text: Overloading is resolved at compile time, from the static types of the arguments, not from the objects they hold at run time. With `label(Object)` and `label(String)`:

items: `Object o = "hi"; label(o)` calls `label(Object)`, because `o` is declared `Object`;
`label(null)` calls `label(String)`, the most specific overload that fits.
`label(Object obj)` returns `"object: "` followed by the object: `label(42)` is `"object: 42"`;
`label(String text)` returns `"text of "` followed by the length: `label("hi")` is `"text of 2"`, and for `null` it returns `"no text"`.

blocks.text: Do not look at the run-time class inside `label(Object)`: a `String` that arrives there was declared as an `Object` by its caller, and is labelled as an object.

cases.says: label("hi") is "text of 2" and label(42) is "object: 42".
A String declared as Object is labelled "object: hi": the compiler chose label(Object).
label(null) is "no text": null picks label(String).

concepts: Overloading is resolved at compile time from the arguments' static types, and null picks the most specific overload.
